title: WestJet denied family's cancelled flight was actually cancelled, claiming passenger rights didn't apply | CBC News
html:
Go Public

WestJet denied family's cancelled flight was actually cancelled, claiming passenger rights didn't apply

Airline reversed course after Go Public got involved

Dustin and Shania Klause's family vacation to Hawaii was thrown into jeopardy after WestJet scrapped their return flight a few months before departure and refused to rebook them on another flight for the same day.

The airline justified its refusal by claiming the flight hadn't been cancelled but, rather, rescheduled — even though it was completely removed from the family's itinerary.

"It's purely a flight cancellation," said a frustrated Dustin, who lives with Shania in Stony Plain, Alta., near Edmonton. "I feel like we were just kind of left in the dust."

The couple had planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, with six family members to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother from ovarian cancer.

"It's just really important to our family to do this together," said Shania. "We had finally had it all worked out."

The family, five adults and three children, planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother. From left to right: Shania's sister-in-law and brother, Tenise and Chad Verbeek; Shania's late mom, Robin Verbeek; Shania's dad, Dale Verbeek; Shania and Dustin Klause. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)

However, in August, WestJet sent an updated itinerary omitting the Kona-to-Vancouver segment of their Nov. 24 return flight to Edmonton — leaving the family without a way home. When Dustin called to complain, the airline offered a replacement return flight departing two days later, which conflicted with several family members' work schedules.

So Dustin, who had researched his rights, insisted WestJet rebook them on another airline for their original travel date — a requirement under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR) for cancellations within an airline's control.

WestJet refused. Multiple customer service agents told Dustin — in calls he recorded — that the regulations didn't apply because the flight disruption was a schedule change.

"If it was a cancellation then, yes, we would be obligated to put you on any carrier we could get you on, but in this case, this is a schedule change," said an agent.

  • Got a story you want investigated? Contact Sophia and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

After Dustin argued repeatedly that his flight had, in fact, been cancelled, the agent replied, "It is considered a schedule-change cancellation. There's a difference."

Not so, according to the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA). Its online guidance states that passenger protection rules apply regardless of how an airline labels a flight disruption.

"A schedule change is effectively a cancellation," said Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, which, for a fee, helps passengers claim flight disruption compensation.

"The flight that you were booked on is gone, and now you're on a different flight."

WestJet reverses course

Airlines have repeatedly flouted Canada's rebooking rules for flight cancellations, resulting in forfeited trips or passengers paying out-of-pocket to salvage their vacations.

WestJet suggested as an option that Dustin accept a refund for the return flight. However, because airfares had increased, Go Public confirmed it would cost the family thousands extra to buy tickets for the same date on another airline.

"We should not have to pay any more money," said Dustin. "At this point, our hands are so tied that we probably have to cancel."

After hearing from Go Public, WestJet reversed course and rebooked the family on their original departure date with partner airline Delta.

"They should have done that from the beginning," said Shania.

WestJet didn't comment directly on Dustin's case except to say that it would offer the family an apology.

The airline also didn't explain why its email notifying the family of the scrapped return flight included refund options under U.S. regulations, but omitted rebooking rights under Canadian regulations.

"Those APPR regulations should be front and centre," said Khan.

$755,000 in fines for rebooking violations

Under the APPR for flight cancellations, major airlines must offer passengers a choice between a refund or rebooking on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline. But if the replacement fight delays travel by more than nine hours — or 48 hours for cancellations outside the airline's control — the carrier must rebook the passenger on any available airline.

Since 2025, the CTA has fined major airlines WestJet, Air Canada, Air Transat, and JetBlue Airways a combined $755,000 for 199 violations of rebooking rules.

Air Canada is challenging its $426,000 penalty for 71 violations last year, arguing the airline was affected by a labour dispute.

Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, says a schedule change is the same as a flight cancellation. (Prasanjeet Choudhury/CBC)

Khan suggests airlines often violate the requirement to rebook on other airlines to cut costs.

"That is the cheapest option, for you to stay on one of their flights," he said. "Unfortunately, most people will accept that."

Under the APPR, passengers are also entitled to up to $1,000 in compensation if an airline cancels a flight for reasons within its control 14 days or less before departure. According to the CTA, airlines have frequently violated this rule as well.

Bigger fines?

To improve compliance with Canada's rebooking rules, Khan supports the federal government's proposal to increase maximum penalties for repeat APPR violations from $25,000 to $1 million.

"I hope no airline has to pay it, but the fact that it exists itself should be a deterrent," said Khan.

However, it's still up in the air whether the new fine limit will be approved, let alone when it would take effect.

Shania and Dustin Klause, far right, are currently enjoying their vacation in Hawaii with family. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)

Meanwhile, Dustin and his family are in Hawaii, relieved that WestJet finally secured them a flight home on their original departure date.

"I'm happy that they actually followed their passenger protection regulations," he said.
summary: A family thought they'd have to cancel a long-awaited trip to Hawaii after WestJet scrapped their return flight. The airline initially refused to rebook them on a same-day flight with another carrier, dismissing the cancellation as a "schedule change."
